name: Tongue splitting

card.summary: Tongue splitting is an extreme body modification that divides the tongue lengthwise into a forked tip, pursued for a distinctive reptilian look and personal expression.
card.aka: Tongue bifurcation, forked tongue, tongue forking
card.note: Bleeding, infection and nerve injury are reported; it is illegal for non-medical practitioners in England and Wales and restricted in several jurisdictions.

quick.overview:
Tongue splitting is a body modification in which the tongue is cut from the tip toward the base so the end forks like a snake's. It sits at the extreme end of the body-modification scene, alongside implants and scarification.

People who do it say it expresses identity, aesthetics or a chosen persona, with some also citing altered sensation. It is not related to conventional attractiveness, and the medical literature on it is mostly case reports and ethics commentary, plus surgical uses of a similar-named approach for unrelated operations.
quick.how: It has been done with a scalpel or laser by a surgeon or modification artist, and in some documented cases by self-performed tie-off methods. Healing is described as taking roughly one to two weeks with difficulty eating and speaking. It can be surgically reversed.
quick.risks: Reported risks include bleeding or hemorrhage, infection, nerve or artery injury, scarring and altered speech sounds. In England and Wales a 2018 Court of Appeal ruling held that cosmetic splitting by a non-medical practitioner is illegal, and several US states and Victoria (Australia) regulate or restrict it.

lead: Tongue splitting, or bifurcation, is a body modification in which the tongue is cut centrally from the tip toward the base, leaving a forked end [1][2]. People pursue it for a reptilian or otherwise distinctive look and for personal reasons such as identity or rites of passage [2].

The modern practice appears in the 1990s: a US piercer split her own tongue in 1996, and sideshow performer Erik Sprague, 'The Lizardman', had a laser split by an oral surgeon in July 1997 [2]. Online body-modification communities spread it [1].

Medical literature consists mainly of case reports, ethics papers and surveys, and a separate surgical literature where 'tongue-splitting approach' means an operative route for tumors or ectopic thyroid, unrelated to the cosmetic procedure [3][4].

chain: Forked tip visible when speaking or showing the tongue
Distinctive reptilian aesthetic and personal identity
angle.text: The procedure changes the shape of the tongue directly, creating a forked tip chosen for its look. It is aimed at a distinctive, subcultural appearance rather than conventional attractiveness.

infobox: Restricted in several jurisdictions; illegal for non-medics in England and Wales [2]

paras: The tongue may be split by scalpel, or by a laser that cauterizes the tissue, with the halves then sutured so they heal separately. Healing generally takes one to two weeks, during which speaking and eating may be hard. Surgeons can reverse a split by removing sutures, excising the healed edges and re-suturing [2]. Splitting can also arise from tongue piercing or as a rare congenital malformation [2].

Some accounts link the idea to yogic khechari mudra, in which the tongue is lengthened, and to ritual tongue piercing in Mesoamerica, though these differ from modern aesthetic splitting [1]. In 1996 Dustin Allor split her own tongue with a tie-off method and appeared on the cover of Body Play Magazine in 1997. Erik Sprague's July 1997 argon-laser procedure by Dr Lawrence Busino, followed by a deeper split in October 1997, brought wider attention [2]. Body Modification Ezine, launched in 1994, helped practitioners share accounts [1]. Hitomi Kanehara's novel Snakes and Earrings used tongue splitting as a motif in Japan [1].

Reasons reported include aesthetics, novelty, belief that it heightens sensation when kissing, group bonding, identity, rites of passage, testing physical limits and spiritual meaning [2]. A survey study of 312 participants linked body modifications, including tongue splitting, with need for uniqueness [5].

Illinois in 2003 was the first US state to regulate it, restricting performance on others to licensed medical practitioners; New York, Delaware and Texas later introduced bans or limits. Victoria banned splitting minors' tongues in 2009. In England and Wales a 2018 Court of Appeal ruling held that cosmetic splitting by a body modification practitioner is unlawful, following the case of Brendan McCarthy, who pleaded guilty in 2019 [2]. Some US military branches prohibit it [2].

No controlled studies of cosmetic tongue splitting exist. The literature includes a 1999 forensic case report on a person with tongue splitting and scarification [6], an ethics paper arguing in its defense on autonomy grounds [7], and a Bioethics paper asking whether extreme modification should be prevented [8]. Reported complications include inflammation, bleeding, infection, injury to nerves or arteries, scar tissue and altered fricative speech sounds [2]. Separately, 'tongue-splitting approach' is a surgical access route used in operations on lingual thyroid and the upper cervical spine [3][4]; those studies do not concern the cosmetic procedure.

timeline.event: Body Modification Ezine launches, later a hub for extreme modification documentation [1].
Erik Sprague's laser splits in July and October [2].
Illinois becomes the first US state to regulate tongue splitting [2].
Victoria, Australia bans splitting minors' tongues [2].
English Court of Appeal rules cosmetic splitting by non-medics unlawful [2].
